readerTitle: The new owners changed nothing big. The regulars left anyway.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 그룹의 비스트로 인수, 급여 대행 회사의 소규모 업체 인수) + 실제 연구 (Haspeslagh & Jemison의 인수 후 통합 유형)
insight: 통합은 두 회사를 똑같이 만드는 일이 아니다. 인수 가치가 걸린 부분만 합치고, 돈을 주고 산 이유는 건드리지 않는 선을 긋는 일이다.
misconception: 인수했으면 빨리 우리 방식으로 다 맞추는 게 효율적이다. 아니면 아예 아무것도 건드리지 않는 게 안전하다.

sources.text: Haspeslagh, P. C. & Jemison, D. B. (1991). Managing Acquisitions: Creating Value Through Corporate Renewal. Free Press.
비스트로와 급여 대행 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Haspeslagh & Jemison(1991)의 틀: 두 축(전략적 상호의존 필요성, 조직 자율성 필요성)과 세 가지 통합 방식(absorption, preservation, symbiosis)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 독자용으로 Absorb / Preserve / Blend라고 풀어 썼습니다.
모든 사업 사례(레스토랑 8곳, 고객 2,000곳·150곳, 6개월 일정 등)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 통계나 실패율 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The new owners changed nothing big. The regulars left anyway.
body: A restaurant group buys a busy neighborhood bistro. It keeps the name, the tables and the staff.
Six months later, the regulars have drifted away. No one made a big change. The group made dozens of small, sensible ones.

image.label: A cozy bistro with half-empty tables and a new corporate binder on the counter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 따뜻한 동네 비스트로 내부. 카운터 위에 두꺼운 '본사 매뉴얼' 바인더가 놓여 있고, 테이블 몇 개가 비어 있음. 창밖으로 단골손님이 지나쳐 가는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: You just bought the bistro.
body: You run eight casual restaurants with shared buying, payroll and menus. You've bought a small bistro famous for its chef's daily fish menu.
Your plan: the bistro grows, and your buying power cuts its costs. What do you change first?

options.text: Bring it fully onto your systems in month one: suppliers, menu, staff rota
options.feedback: You get savings fast and one way of working. But the chef and the daily menu are what you paid for, and they may not survive group rules.

options.text: Change nothing for a year so you don't break anything
options.feedback: The magic stays safe, but the savings you planned never arrive, and staff sit in limbo wondering what's coming.

options.text: Move payroll, accounting and dry-goods buying now; leave the chef, fish suppliers and menu alone
options.feedback: You capture savings where customers never notice them. Where you draw that line is the whole lesson.

cards.title: Each change made sense. Together they didn't.
body: Picture the group that chose A. Its standard supplier was cheaper, so the fish changed. Its menu software needed dishes set a week ahead, so the daily menu became weekly. Its pricing rules pushed the wine list down a tier.
Every change saved money on paper. Together they removed the reason people came. Then the chef left, and the regulars followed her.

cards.title: Integration
body: **Integration** is the work of combining two businesses after one buys the other: which systems, teams, suppliers and habits become shared, which stay separate, and how fast.
The price is fixed on signing day. Whether the deal was worth it is decided in the months after, one integration choice at a time.

image.label: Two kitchens joined by a shared back office, with a dotted line around one stove
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 두 주방이 가운데 공통 사무실(급여, 회계, 구매)로 연결되어 있고, 한쪽 주방의 셰프 화덕 주변만 점선으로 보호 구역 표시 'Keep'. 공통 사무실에는 'Combine' 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Two questions, three paths.
body: Researchers Philippe Haspeslagh and David Jemison framed it as two questions. How much does the deal's value depend on combining things? And how much does the bought business need its independence to stay valuable?

breakdown.label: Combine almost everything
breakdown.detail: Value comes from combining; little to protect

breakdown.label: Keep it largely separate
breakdown.detail: Value lives in its people and ways of working

cards.callout: The bistro is a blend: share the back office, protect the kitchen.

cards.title: Start with what you paid for.
body: A practical way to draw the line:
list: **What you paid for** (people, recipes, relationships, reputation): protect it, sometimes in writing.
**What you bought it to combine** (buying, systems, customer lists): integrate it quickly and clearly.
**Everything else:** leave it until there's a real reason to change.
cards.softwareNote: When a software company buys a smaller product, the pull is to fold it into the main app, login and pricing. If users chose it for its simplicity, folding it in can break it. Share accounts and billing; keep the product team and its design choices.

cards.title: Leaving things alone isn't free.
body: Every separate system, supplier and process costs money to run. Protect too much and the deal becomes an expensive asset you can't improve.
Slowness costs too. People who don't know what will change start looking for other jobs. Decide the line early, say it plainly, and move fast on the parts you will combine.

cards.title: Now it's payroll services.
body: Your firm runs payroll for 2,000 businesses through a central service team. You buy a small firm with 150 restaurant clients. They stay because each has one named person who answers the phone.
You want to sell them your benefits services too. What do you integrate?

options.text: Move the clients to your central team so everyone gets the same service
options.feedback: Efficient, but the named person is what those clients pay for. Many may leave before you sell them anything.

options.text: Keep the named account managers; move payroll processing and billing onto your systems over six months
options.feedback: Clients keep the relationship they value, and you gain the shared systems that make savings and cross-selling possible.

options.text: Run the firm fully separately, on its own systems, indefinitely
options.feedback: The clients stay happy, but you pay for two of everything, and your benefits services have no easy way in.

cards.title: Integrate what the deal needs. Protect what you paid for.
body: A deal's value is won or lost after signing. Before changing anything in a business you buy, name the few things customers come for, and keep your hands off them.
**Try it today:** think of a team, supplier or business you've merged with or joined. List what made it valuable and what got combined. Did any change touch the first list?
